reason: The text depicts King Saul's antagonism toward David specifically, not toward the Hebrew people broadly. While Saul does seek David's death (מְבַקֵּשׁ אֶת־ נַפְשִׁי) and becomes enraged with him, this is a personal/political conflict. Conversely, Jonathan, another Hebrew leader and Saul's own son, is portrayed as David's devoted protector and friend (וַיְהִ֗י כְּכַלֹּתוֹ֙ לְדַבֵּ֣ר אֶל־ שָׁא֔וּל וְנֶ֙פֶשׁ֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן נִקְשְׁרָ֖ה בְּנֶ֣פֶשׁ דָּוִ֑ד). He consistently intercedes for David's safety and loyalty. The statement overgeneralizes: while one leader (Saul) opposes one person (David), the text does not support the broad claim that Hebrew leaders as a category are antagonistic to the people as a category.
